event: Elsie wakes to the smell of bread from four o'clock, and lies still, humming last night's tune.
She sits up and writes to her mother: a Berserker, an Alchemist, and a Warden who watches her.
She waters the four plants one by one and tells them the party goes out at dusk for moonbells.
She laces the cream halter, clips the flower above one ear, and checks the salve and bandages.
Downstairs the baker gives her a warm roll and asks about the Naming; Elsie says Enthraller.
The baker is quiet a moment, and then puts a second roll in her hand and tells her to eat.
At the flower market she buys a pair of thick gloves and a canvas bag that will hold plants.
At a chandler's stall she buys a lantern and a flask of oil and a coil of thin rope.
She buys bread and cheese and apples for four and a paper twist of salt.
On Mortar Lane the apothecary's shop is shut, with the moonbell notice pasted in the window.
The apothecary comes down and tells her the delivery is wanted by morning, not by noon.
Elsie says she has never been inside a dungeon, and the apothecary says come back alive then.
The party board is busy, and the last slate still carries the three chalked names.
Somebody has rubbed out and written the names on the Leftovers' slates twice already.
Tamsin is not at the hall yet, so Elsie reads the F-rank notices again, all the way down.
Pickle Row smells of sulphur; Tilly's landlady points her up two flights and shuts her door.
Tilly's room is one bench of bubbling glass, a bed she has not made, and no floor to see.
Tilly says she has been up since four, and has made three of everything, and none of it works.
Elsie asks what the three things are; Tilly names a stink bomb, a burn salve and a fizz.
Elsie says the salve is the one she wants for the Glasswood, and Tilly goes red to the ears.
Tilly packs the salve and four vials and a coiled fuse she says is for noise and not for them.
Elsie asks about the College; Tilly talks fast for a while and then stops in the middle.
Elsie says her mother was thrown out of nothing, being a caravan healer, and Tilly laughs.
They walk out together; Tilly wears the apron and says the goggles are for the glass.
Tilly reads the board's small print and finds the line about the white posts and the mile.
The docks smell of tar; Tamsin's lodging house has a door that does not shut behind them.
Tamsin comes down with her hair wet and Margery over her shoulder, and stops on the step.
Elsie holds out the bread she bought; Tamsin takes it and says she was going to eat anyway.
They sit on the quay; Tamsin eats the whole loaf and gives the crust to a barge cat.
Elsie asks about the Frenzy; Tamsin says it comes on when her blood is up and she blacks out.
Tamsin says what she does inside it is not hers, and the parties are right to drop her.
Elsie asks what to do if it comes; Tamsin says do not run, and do not stand in front of her.
Elsie asks what helps; Tamsin says nothing has ever been tried, and nothing would.
Elsie says she has never used her class on anyone and does not know whether it would help.
Tamsin looks at her a long moment and says, we will see about that.
Cora is waiting at the guild hall with the ledger under her arm and no greeting for either.
Cora says she will walk the Glasswood's edge with them and log the party in and out.
Elsie asks whether Cora has been to the edge; Cora says on Wardens' patrols, and knows it.
Elsie asks what grows in the hollows; Cora says moonbells, and glass, and thornhares.
Elsie asks about the wolves; Cora says on summer nights a pack hunts the edge of the wood.
Cora says they fear fire and noise and go for whoever runs, and writes none of it down.
Elsie asks what Cora will write; Cora says she has not decided, and opens the door for her.
Elsie asks what the guild does about a first skill; Cora says it is reported, not punished.
Cora says the Accord is not there to catch her, whatever she thinks Wardens are for.
Elsie says she is glad Cora is coming; Cora says that is not the part of it she is in.
Elsie fills the satchel at the attic: the salve, the bandages, bread, the lantern and the rope.
She clips the flower straight, and puts the apothecary's coin in the pocket she can reach.
She rests on the bed with the round window open, listening to the boats on the canal.
She dozes, and wakes with last night's hum already going, and cannot stop it.
At the hall the four of them check over what each is bringing, on the long table.
Tilly shows the fuses, Tamsin a tinderbox, Cora nothing, and Elsie the rope and the lantern.
Tamsin says the clerk's booth closes at dark, so they go an hour before it, as she said.
Tilly asks what the white posts mean; Tamsin says they are as far as F-rank may go.
Elsie asks to hold Margery; Tamsin lends her the axe and watches her hands the whole time.
Elsie gives it back and says it is heavier than she looks; Tamsin says everything is.
They cross the south canal bridge to the east gate as the lamplighters start their round.
The clerk's booth at the gate is lit, and he takes their names and their copper tags.
Cora gives the names; the clerk writes the party into the book and sells them a licence.
The clerk says F-rank goes a mile in and no farther, and the white posts are the line.
Outside the gate the cart track runs east between meadows, with marsh birds calling.
The four of them walk east with the lantern, and the city light drops away behind them.
Tamsin says she has been out here a dozen times, and past the white posts twice.
Tilly asks what the twice was like; Tamsin says it was quick, both times.
Elsie asks what lies past the posts; Tamsin says more wood, and nobody to tell her no.
The glass trees begin at the first hollow, and knock together overhead in the wind.
At the wood's edge the chiming goes through her teeth, and Elsie laughs out loud.
Elsie tells them the hour, and the moonbells lie shut and blue among the tree roots.
They spread along the edge with the lantern low and their gloves on, and wait for dusk.
Dusk comes and the bells open all together, and the hollow fills with a pale blue light.
Elsie picks with two fingers and the stems come clean; Tilly picks and drops the first one.
Tamsin gathers with the axe out of the way and her back to the wood, watching the trees.
Cora stands where she can see the hollow and the wood both, and writes the hour down.
The satchel takes the bells by handfuls, and Elsie keeps the lantern up and the talk light.
Tilly asks whether these are the right blue; Elsie says the blue ones are the ones at dusk.
By full dark the edge hollows are picked, and the satchel is heavier than it looks.
Tamsin says one hollow more and they are done; the fourth lies back under the trees.
They go in single file, and the glass underfoot grinds like sugar the whole way in.
The first wolf comes out of the trees without a sound, lamp-eyed, and the pack after it.
Tilly drops her basket; the lantern goes over and guttering, and the wood goes dark.
Tamsin tells them to stand still and swings; the pack circles wide and one goes for Tilly.
Tamsin's axe takes it across the shoulder, and the others come at her out of the trees.
Elsie sees Tamsin's face change, and knows what is coming and has no word for it.
Tamsin turns on the hollow, and the axe comes round with the whole length of her arms.
Cora pulls Tilly out of the swing; the axe bites the glass trunk and the tree rings.
Tamsin is gone into it: she does not know them, and the pack is between her and them.
Tamsin shouts for the fuses; Tilly throws two, and the bramblewolves flinch back.
Elsie walks toward Tamsin with the lantern and puts her hand flat on Tamsin's jaw.
Elsie says her name and says she is here; a window opens above them and reads: Captivate.
Tamsin's eyes come back to her, the axe drops, and Tamsin shakes like a struck bell.
The pack breaks at the noise and the light and the two of them standing still in it.
Cora takes up the axe, Tilly counts the party twice, and Elsie does not let go of her.
In the ranger's hut the lantern is lit and Tilly wraps the cut on Tamsin's arm.
Tamsin will not look at anybody and says she is sorry, and the hut stays quiet.
Elsie says the wolves are gone and the bells are in the satchel and they are all here.
Cora opens the black ledger on the hut table and writes in it, in her small exact hand.
Elsie asks what she wrote; Cora says what the Accord asks for, and nothing but that.
They come back through the east gate and the clerk writes the party out of his book.
The canals are lit end to end; Tamsin carries the satchel and Tilly sleeps on her feet.
At the apothecary's door on Mortar Lane they hand over the bells, and are paid on the step.
Elsie walks home under the lanterns, her hands still smelling of the blue flowers.
